subject: chemistry
title: Halogenoalkanes and nucleophilic substitution
key_idea: A halogenoalkane has a polar carbon–halogen bond. The δ+ carbon is attacked by nucleophiles, which replace the halogen. The weaker the carbon–halogen bond, the faster the reaction. Primary, secondary and tertiary halogenoalkanes differ in how they react.

blocks.text: Halogenoalkanes are alkanes with one or more hydrogen atoms replaced by a halogen. This section covers their polar bond and how they are classified.

items: The halogen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is **polar**.
The carbon carries a partial positive charge (δ+). The halogen carries a partial negative charge (δ–).
The δ+ carbon is the site that nucleophiles attack.

blocks.text: A nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbon and replaces the halogen. This is nucleophilic substitution. This section covers the reagents and conditions.

items.meaning: An electron pair donor. It uses a lone pair to form a new covalent bond.
A reaction in which a nucleophile replaces an atom or group on a molecule.
A reaction with water or hydroxide ions that breaks a bond and adds OH.

Example: CH₃CH₂Br + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CN + Br⁻. The new C–C bond makes the carbon chain longer.
Example: CH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br. A second ammonia molecule removes H⁺.

blocks.text: Water is a weak nucleophile, so hydrolysis with silver nitrate is slow. The halide ion that leaves is at once precipitated by Ag⁺. The colour of the precipitate shows which halogen was present.

options.label: Chloroalkane
results: Slowest. The C–Cl bond is the strongest of the three.

options.label: Iodoalkane
results: Fastest. The C–I bond is the weakest.

items: A nucleophile donates a lone pair to the δ+ carbon.
Aqueous hydroxide gives an alcohol, cyanide a nitrile and ammonia an amine.
Silver nitrate in ethanol shows which halogen is present, from the colour of the precipitate.

blocks.text: Primary halogenoalkanes react in one step, called SN₂. This section covers the mechanism using hydroxide as the nucleophile.

items.text: The hydroxide ion uses a lone pair on oxygen to attack the δ+ carbon, from the side opposite the halogen.
A curly arrow goes from the lone pair on OH⁻ to the carbon. A second curly arrow goes from the C–Br bond to the bromine atom.
A new C–O bond forms as the C–Br bond breaks. The products are an alcohol and a bromide ion, Br⁻.

items: The same mechanism works with CN⁻ and with NH₃ as the nucleophile.
With ammonia the first product is an ion, RNH₃⁺. A second ammonia removes H⁺ to give RNH₂.
Curly arrows start from a lone pair or a bond and end at the atom that receives the pair.
Primary halogenoalkanes react by a one-step mechanism.
The curly arrow from the nucleophile starts at its lone pair.

blocks.text: The rate of hydrolysis depends on the halogen and on the type of halogenoalkane. This section explains each trend.

items: The C–X bond must break in the rate-determining step.
The bond gets weaker down the group: C–F is strongest and C–I is weakest. Approximate values are C–Cl 346, C–Br 290 and C–I 228 kJ/mol.
Less energy is needed to break the bond, so the rate of hydrolysis increases: RCl < RBr < RI.
Bond polarity is not the deciding factor. C–F is the most polar bond but the slowest to react.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes hydrolyse fastest. Primary are slowest. Secondary lie between.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes form a more stable carbocation, because three alkyl groups push electron density towards the positive carbon.
Alkyl groups also hinder the approach of a nucleophile, which slows the one-step mechanism for tertiary compounds.
Weaker C–X bonds react faster, so iodoalkanes are the most reactive.
The order of hydrolysis rate is tertiary, then secondary, then primary.

checks.q: State what is meant by the term nucleophile and give two examples.
checks.a: An electron pair donor. Examples: OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃ or H₂O.

checks.q: 1-bromopropane is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Write the equation and name the type of mechanism and the organic product.
checks.a: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + Br⁻. Nucleophilic substitution. The product is propan-1-ol.

checks.q: Explain why 1-iodobutane is hydrolysed faster than 1-chlorobutane.
checks.a: The C–I bond is weaker (has a lower bond enthalpy) than the C–Cl bond. Less energy is needed to break it, so the reaction is faster.

items: Compare rates of hydrolysis experimentally. Warm the halogenoalkane in ethanol with aqueous silver nitrate at the same temperature.
Time how long the precipitate takes to appear. A shorter time means a faster reaction.
Explain the trend for C–F, C–Cl, C–Br and C–I in terms of bond enthalpy. C–F is so strong that it hardly reacts.
Know the mechanism for the hydrolysis of a primary halogenoalkane with aqueous alkali.
In the silver nitrate reaction, water acts as the nucleophile. The reaction compares chloro-, bromo- and iodoalkanes, and also primary, secondary and tertiary compounds.
Experimental data can show the order: iodoalkane > bromoalkane > chloroalkane, and tertiary > secondary > primary.
Know the reaction with potassium cyanide as an example of lengthening the carbon chain.
Know the mechanisms for primary halogenoalkanes with aqueous potassium hydroxide and with ammonia.
Know that ethanolic potassium hydroxide makes an alkene, where hydroxide acts as a base. This is covered under elimination.
Outline the nucleophilic substitution mechanisms with OH⁻, CN⁻ and NH₃.
With ammonia, draw the intermediate in which nitrogen has a positive charge, then show a second ammonia molecule removing H⁺.
Explain why the carbon–halogen bond enthalpy influences the rate of reaction.
From alkanes: free-radical substitution with Cl₂ or Br₂ and ultraviolet light, for example C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl.
From alkenes: electrophilic addition of X₂ or HX(g) at room temperature.
From alcohols: substitution using HX(g); KCl with concentrated H₂SO₄ or concentrated H₃PO₄; PCl₃ and heat; PCl₅; or SOCl₂.

blocks.text: SN stands for substitution, nucleophilic. The number is the molecularity of the rate-determining step: 2 means two species collide in it, 1 means only one.

items.text: The nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbon as the C–X bond breaks. The transition state has both the nucleophile and the halogen partly bonded. The rate depends on both reactants.
The C–X bond breaks heterolytically, slowly, to give a carbocation and X⁻. The rate depends only on the halogenoalkane.
The nucleophile attacks the planar carbocation and bonds to the carbon quickly.

items: Primary halogenoalkanes tend to react by SN₂. Tertiary react by SN₁. Secondary react by a mixture of the two, depending on structure.
Alkyl groups are electron-donating (the inductive effect). Three of them stabilise the tertiary carbocation, which favours SN₁.
Bulky alkyl groups around the carbon also block the nucleophile, which disfavours SN₂.
Reactions with NaOH(aq) and heat give an alcohol, KCN in ethanol and heat a nitrile, and NH₃ in ethanol heated under pressure an amine.
